subject: Copywriting
title: David Ogilvy: The King of Long Copy
description: A micro-lesson that makes David Ogilvy: The King of Long Copy usable.

hook.text: 'At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock.' Ogilvy's most famous.

buildup.text: Ogilvy built Ogilvy & Mather into a global powerhouse. He believed advertising should sell, not just entertain.

discovery.text: He championed long-form copy. His Rolls-Royce ad had 607 words. His research showed long copy outsold short.

twist.text: Ogilvy was a chef, farmer, and spy before advertising. He entered the industry at 38 with zero experience.

climax.text: His book 'Ogilvy on Advertising' is still required reading. His rules for headlines and body copy are timeless.

punchline.text: A spy became the king of advertising. Long copy sold cars.

quiz.question: How many words did Ogilvy's famous Rolls-Royce ad contain?

details.summary: David Ogilvy founded Ogilvy & Mather and championed research-driven, long-form copywriting that respected the reader's intelligence. His campaigns for Rolls-Royce, Hathaway Shirts, and Dove established him as the most famous advertising figure of the twentieth century.
details.whyItMatters: Ogilvy proved that long copy sells when it is well-researched and well-written. His rules for effective advertising remain the most-cited guidelines in the industry.
takeaways: Ogilvy's Rolls-Royce headline is among the most celebrated ads ever written
He insisted that research must precede creativity in advertising
His book 'Ogilvy on Advertising' remains an industry standard

faq.question: What is Ogilvy's most famous advertisement?
faq.answer: His Rolls-Royce ad with the headline 'At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock' is widely considered the greatest print ad ever written. It combined a specific factual claim with elegant prose.

faq.question: Why did Ogilvy believe long copy was effective?
faq.answer: Ogilvy argued that people who are interested in a product will read every word, and people who are not interested won't read even a short ad. Long copy gives interested prospects the information they need to buy, which consistently outperformed short copy in his tests.
